summary: A sultan's tomb, a college and a free hospital built in about a year; the hospital went on treating Cairenes for more than 500 years.
look: On the west side of Bayn al-Qasrayn, a façade about 67 metres long with tall pointed-arch panels, a minaret by the entrance and a striped arch over the door. A long corridor runs inside, with the madrasa on your left and the mausoleum on your right; the hospital lay beyond. The mausoleum is the room not to miss: piers and columns in an octagon under a high dome, walls of marble mosaic and carved stucco, and painted, gilded ceilings.
story:
Qalawun was a mamluk, a Kipchak Turk bought as a slave soldier, who became sultan in 1279 and beat the Mongols at the Second Battle of Homs. His descendants held the throne, with interruptions, for about a century. In 1284 he began his funerary complex on the ruins of the Fatimid Western Palace, and the speed was astonishing: the hospital went up in under six months, and the whole complex took about thirteen.

The speed had a price. The historian al-Maqrizi says the overseer, the emir Sanjar al-Shuja'i, used forced labour, including Mongol prisoners, seized property and evicted residents, and some scholars urged a boycott of the building. The columns of the mausoleum reportedly came from the palace of Qalawun's old master, al-Salih, on Roda Island.

The bimaristan, or hospital, was the heart of the gift. Al-Maqrizi says Qalawun had once fallen ill in Damascus, been treated in Nur al-Din's hospital there, and vowed to build one. Its endowment paid for treatment, medicines, food, clothing and the teaching of medicine. It kept working into the late Ottoman period, more than 500 years, before most of it was demolished in 1910.

The mausoleum holds Qalawun and his son al-Nasir Muhammad. Four piers and four columns form an octagon under the dome, a plan many historians compare with the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. New emirs were invested here, beside the founder's tomb. The dome itself is a 1908 reconstruction, after an earlier Ottoman rebuild by Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda.
details: The façade: tall pointed-arch panels framing windows, which scholars compare to Gothic work of the Crusader period.
Mausoleum: four piers and four columns in an octagon carrying the dome, the plan likened to the Dome of the Rock.
The mausoleum mihrab, often called the most lavish in Cairo: a horseshoe niche framed by marble columns.
The madrasa mihrab, left of the corridor: glass and mother-of-pearl mosaic in deep red, with scrolling vines.
The minaret by the entrance: three storeys, rebuilt by al-Nasir Muhammad after the 1302 earthquake.
fun_fact: The tomb chamber was also a ceremonial stage: new Mamluk emirs were invested here, swearing loyalty beside the founder of the dynasty.
narration: This long facade belongs to the complex of Sultan Qalawun: a mausoleum, a college and, behind them, one of the great hospitals of the Middle Ages. Qalawun was a mamluk, a Turkish slave soldier who became sultan in 1279 and founded a dynasty that held the throne for about a century. He built all this in 1284 and 1285, astonishingly fast: the hospital in less than six months, the whole complex in about thirteen. The speed had a price. A chronicler tells us the overseer used forced labour, including Mongol prisoners, and threw people out of their houses, and some scholars urged a boycott. The hospital, though, was a real gift. Qalawun had once been treated in a hospital in Damascus and vowed to build one himself. Here patients received treatment, medicine, food and clothes, all paid for by the endowment, and it kept working for more than 500 years. Inside, the corridor leads to the mausoleum on your right. Qalawun lies here, and so does his son al-Nasir Muhammad. Look up at the ring of columns and piers carrying the dome: many historians see in it an echo of the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem.

summary: Its marble doorway is a Gothic church portal, carried off from Acre after the last great Crusader city fell in 1291 and set up here as a trophy.
look: Squeezed between Qalawun and Barquq, a narrow façade with a white marble Gothic portal: a pointed arch with triple recesses and slender colonettes. Right above the door rises the minaret, its lowest storey covered in fine carved stucco. Inside, little survives but the stucco mihrab; the dome over the tomb fell in 1870 and was never rebuilt.
story:
The madrasa was begun around 1295 by Sultan al-Adil Kitbugha, who had pushed aside the boy sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. When al-Nasir returned to power he finished it and inaugurated it in 1303. The façade inscription still carries the original foundation date: he simply had his own name put in place of Kitbugha's.

The portal comes from Acre. In 1291 Qalawun's son al-Ashraf Khalil captured the city, the last great Crusader stronghold, and sent the emir Sanjar al-Shuja'i to demolish its walls and churches. The emir had this portal taken down and moved intact to Cairo. Which church it came from is disputed: St Andrew, St Agnes and St John the Baptist have all been proposed. Kitbugha seized it and installed it here, a trophy of the end of the Crusades.

Al-Nasir Muhammad became sultan at nine in 1293, lost the throne twice, and ruled for real from 1310 to 1341, the high point of Mamluk Cairo. He was not buried here: fearing unrest, his emirs buried him secretly in his father's mausoleum next door. This tomb holds his mother and his son Anuk.
details: The apex of the Gothic arch: the word Allah carved into a Christian church portal.
The minaret's lower storey: dense stucco medallions and keel-arched niches, possibly by North African or Andalusian craftsmen.
Inside, the stucco mihrab, the last of its kind in Egypt, close in style to work from Tabriz in Mongol Iran.
Look up in the tomb chamber: the dome fell in 1870, and a plain wooden roof replaced it.
fun_fact: This is one of only three madrasas in Cairo that taught all four schools of Sunni law under one roof.
narration: Look at this doorway carefully, because it is a Gothic church portal. In 1291 the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil captured Acre, the last great Crusader city on the coast of Palestine. One of his emirs demolished its walls and churches and had this marble portal taken down and carried intact to Cairo. Historians still argue which church it came from. A few years later Sultan Kitbugha set it up here, in front of his new madrasa, as a trophy of victory. Kitbugha had pushed aside the boy sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, son of Qalawun. But al-Nasir came back, finished the building in 1303, and simply had his own name carved in place of Kitbugha's. During his third reign, which lasted until 1341, Cairo reached its peak. He is not buried here, though: he was laid secretly in his father's tomb next door. Now look up to the top of the pointed arch. Right at its apex, carved into a Christian portal, is the word Allah.

summary: Built by the first Circassian sultan, a former slave who lost his throne and won it back, it hides one of Cairo's finest painted ceilings.
look: The northernmost of the three great façades of Bayn al-Qasrayn, with a tall portal and bronze-plated doors patterned with stars. A vaulted vestibule leads to a courtyard with four iwans and striped stone. The largest iwan, the prayer hall, is divided by reused ancient columns into three aisles under a painted and gilded wooden ceiling; the domed tomb chamber opens off it.
story:
Barquq was a Circassian from the Caucasus, enslaved as a boy and bought into the household of the emir Yalbugha around 1363. In November 1382 he deposed the last of Qalawun's line and took the throne, opening the Circassian, or Burji, period of Mamluk rule. In 1389 rebels captured him and locked him in the castle of Kerak, in today's Jordan, but he was back in Cairo by February 1390 and reigned until his death in 1399.

The façade inscription dates the building from December 1384 to April 1386. The supervisor was Jarkas al-Khalili, the emir who founded Khan el-Khalili, and the architect Ahmad al-Tuluni, whose relatives Barquq married. The workers were paid, unlike Qalawun's. The foundation deed lists a Friday mosque, a college teaching the four Sunni law schools to 125 students, and a khanqah, a lodge for sixty Sufis.

The tomb chamber holds Barquq's daughter Fatima, and his father's remains were moved here. Barquq himself lies in the Northern Cemetery, in the great khanqah completed by his son Faraj. Thieves stripped much of the ornament from the minbar and the door in 2012 and 2013.
details: The bronze-plated doors: geometric patterns built on 18- and 12-pointed stars.
Around the doorway: a Quranic inscription whose letter tops are knotted like flowers.
The prayer hall ceiling: painted and gilded wood like an illuminated Quran page, the largest single Mamluk wooden roof.
The marble floor of the prayer hall, with mosaic panels shaped like little mihrabs.
The tomb chamber: the dome was rebuilt in 1893, but the wooden pendentives at its base are original.
fun_fact: The emir who supervised this building, Jarkas al-Khalili, is the same man whose khan gave Khan el-Khalili its name, a few minutes' walk away.
narration: This is the madrasa and khanqah of Sultan Barquq, finished in 1386. Barquq was a Circassian from the Caucasus, sold as a boy into slavery, and in 1382 he became the first of a new line of Mamluk sultans. His career had a twist: in 1389 rebels overthrew him and locked him in the castle of Kerak, in today's Jordan, but within a year he was back on the throne. The building did three jobs. It was a Friday mosque, a college for 125 students of Islamic law, and a khanqah, a lodge where 60 Sufi mystics lived and prayed on a stipend. The man who supervised the work was Jarkas al-Khalili, the same emir who gave his name to Khan el-Khalili. The domed tomb holds Barquq's daughter, not Barquq himself: he lies in the Northern Cemetery, in a complex finished by his son. Walk through to the prayer hall and look up. The painted and gilded wooden ceiling, patterned like a page of an illuminated Quran, is the largest single wooden roof of the Mamluk age.

summary: The last great Mamluk sultan built a mosque and a tomb facing each other across the street, then died in battle and never lay in his tomb.
look: Just south of al-Azhar Street, two buildings face each other across al-Muizz, joined by a wooden roof over the cloth market between them. On the west stands the mosque-madrasa with its tall square minaret; on the east, the mausoleum and Sufi hall, with a sabil-kuttab on the corner. His caravanserai, the Wikala al-Ghuri, is a short walk east along al-Azhar Street.
story:
Qansuh al-Ghuri ruled from 1501 to 1516. He had been governor of Tarsus and chamberlain of Aleppo, loved music, poetry, flowers and Sufis, and paid for his showcase buildings partly by confiscating property. His mosque opened with a banquet in May 1503; relics of the Prophet were moved into the mausoleum in 1504. The tomb's dome was covered in tiles described as lapis blue, so unstable that it was rebuilt in 1512-13 and finally pulled down in 1860.

In 1516 he marched north against the Ottoman sultan Selim I. At Marj Dabiq near Aleppo his governor Khayrbak changed sides mid-battle, the old sultan collapsed and died, and his body was never found. Within months the Ottomans held Cairo, and Selim shipped the building's marble to Istanbul.

Nearby, the Wikala al-Ghuri (1504-05) rises five storeys round a courtyard: animals and goods on the ground floor, merchants above, and three floors of rented apartments on top. Its rents helped pay for the complex. Today it houses craft workshops and evening shows of Sufi whirling, the tannoura.
details: The minaret: a square shaft ending in five little domed heads, a 19th-century replacement for al-Ghuri's original four.
The sabil-kuttab on the corner of the eastern building: water below, school above, marble star paving inside.
Under the wooden roof: clothes and cloth stalls continue the textile market whose rents paid for the buildings.
Wikala al-Ghuri: five storeys round a courtyard. The tannoura show runs only on certain evenings, so check; the 16th is a Friday.
fun_fact: In 1945 the young civil servant Naguib Mahfouz asked to be posted to the library in this mausoleum, and used the job to interview people from his old neighbourhood.
narration: The two buildings facing each other here are the complex of Qansuh al-Ghuri, the last great Mamluk sultan, built between 1503 and 1505. On one side is his mosque and college, with the tall square minaret. On the other is his mausoleum and a hall for Sufis. The wooden roof between them shades the cloth market, whose rents helped pay for it all. Al-Ghuri loved music, poetry and flowers, and he paid for his buildings partly by confiscating other people's property. In 1516 he marched north to fight the Ottoman sultan Selim. Near Aleppo, in the middle of the battle, one of his governors switched sides. The old sultan collapsed and died, and his body was never found. So the splendid tomb he built here never received him. A few months later the Ottomans took Cairo. A short walk east is his caravanserai, the Wikala al-Ghuri, where Sufi whirling dancers perform on some evenings. Now look up at the minaret: its top ends in a cluster of little domed heads, a late Mamluk flourish.

summary: A sultan who once suffered in a prison here tore it down and built his mosque on the spot, with two minarets planted on top of the city gate.
look: Bab Zuwayla is the southern gate of the Fatimid city: two rounded stone towers with a vaulted passage between them, topped since 1419-1420 by the two slim minarets of the mosque next door. The mosque of al-Mu'ayyad stands just inside the gate on the west side of the street, its tall façade and great bronze door facing al-Muizz. A ticket usually lets you climb onto the gate and up the minarets.
story:
The vizier Badr al-Jamali built the gate in 1092, naming it after Fatimid soldiers of the Zawila Berber tribe from the Libyan Sahara. For centuries it was Cairo's place of execution. In 1260 Sultan Qutuz hung the heads of Mongol envoys here before marching to victory at Ain Jalut. In 1517 the Ottomans hanged Tumanbay, the last Mamluk sultan, in this gateway; the story goes that the rope broke twice.

Al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh, bought as a boy by Sultan Barquq, was once jailed in a prison on this site. Al-Maqrizi says he suffered from fleas and lice there and vowed to turn it into a place of learning if he ever came to power. He took the throne in 1412, demolished the prison, and from 1415 built this mosque and college for 40,000 dinars, perching its two minarets on the gate's towers. Inscriptions inside them name the builder, Muhammad ibn al-Qazzaz. He also took the bronze door and a chandelier from Sultan Hassan's mosque. He lies in the domed mausoleum with his son.

Later the gate gained a saint, Mitwalli al-Qutb, and people nailed hair or scraps of clothing to its doors to ask for help against illness.
details: The gate's wooden doors: each leaf weighs about three and a half tonnes.
The mosque's bronze-covered door: made for Sultan Hassan's mosque, taken by al-Mu'ayyad.
The mausoleum dome beside the gate: carved stone with a zigzag pattern, typical of the early 1400s.
From the minaret tops: al-Muizz Street running north, and the Citadel and Muhammad Ali's mosque to the south-east.
fun_fact: The prisoner kept his vow with interest: the lice-ridden jail became one of 15th-century Cairo's leading colleges, where the great scholar Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani taught law.
narration: In front of you is Bab Zuwayla, the southern gate of Fatimid Cairo, built in 1092 and named after a regiment of Berber soldiers from the Libyan desert who camped here. For centuries this was where Cairo hanged criminals and displayed heads. In 1260 the Mamluk sultan hung the heads of Mongol envoys here before beating the Mongols in battle. And in 1517 the conquering Ottomans hanged the last Mamluk sultan, Tumanbay, in this gateway; the story goes that the rope broke twice. The two minarets on top belong to the mosque next door. Its founder, Sultan al-Muayyad, had once been a prisoner in a jail on this very spot, tormented by fleas and lice. He swore that if he ever came to power he would turn the prison into a holy place. He did, between 1415 and 1421, and he even took his great bronze door from the mosque of Sultan Hassan. If the ticket office is open, climb up to the minarets: from the top you look straight down al-Muizz Street, the whole Fatimid city at your feet.

summary: Medieval Cairo's biggest and most expensive mosque, paid for partly with the estates of plague victims, and so massive it served as a fortress.
look: Facing the Citadel across the square, a cliff of stone about 150 metres long, 68 wide and 36 high. The entrance portal rises 38 metres, and much of its decoration was never finished. Inside, a dark bent passage opens into a huge courtyard with four vaulted iwans; the biggest, facing Mecca, has the domed mausoleum directly behind it. The surviving tall minaret reaches about 84 metres above the street.
story:
An-Nasir Hasan, a son of al-Nasir Muhammad, became sultan at thirteen in 1347, a puppet of his emirs. He was deposed in 1351 and held for three years, returned to power, and in 1361 was murdered by his own mamluk Yalbugha al-Umari. His body was never found.

Work began in 1356, in the years after the Black Death had swept Cairo. The money came from austerity, from the seized estates of plague-killed emirs and from extortion. Al-Maqrizi says it cost 30,000 dirhams a day and over a million dinars in all, the most expensive mosque of medieval Cairo. Craftsmen came from across the empire, including Anatolia, and limestone is believed to have been quarried from the Giza pyramids.

The four iwans are said to have housed the four Sunni law schools, and each corner hides its own madrasa with a courtyard and four storeys of student cells. Unusually, the mausoleum sits right behind the qibla wall; it holds two of Hassan's young sons. In 1361 one of four planned minarets collapsed and killed around 300 people, including children at a school below, and the plan was abandoned.

The building's size and position made it a fortress. In 1391 Barquq had the entrance stairs destroyed and the door blocked; in 1517 Tumanbay held out inside while the Ottomans bombarded it from the Citadel, and a 1660 account describes the dome full of cannonball holes.
details: The portal: look high up for patterns drawn onto the stone but never carved out, left as they were in the 1360s.
The long chains hanging in the iwans once held enamelled glass lamps; originals survive in museums.
The qibla iwan's band of Kufic script: the Quran's chapter of Victory, running round the hall.
Through a door beside the mihrab: the mausoleum, with Hassan's two sons buried under the dome.
Doors in the courtyard corners lead into the four madrasas: peek in at the cells stacked several storeys high.
fun_fact: The bronze-covered door you would once have walked through is now on al-Mu'ayyad's mosque by Bab Zuwayla: in the early 1400s that sultan acquired it for a modest price.
narration: You are standing under Sultan Hassan, the largest and most expensive mosque of medieval Cairo, built between 1356 and 1363. Hassan became sultan at thirteen, a puppet of his emirs, and was murdered in 1361; his body was never found. How did he pay for this? Partly with death. The Black Death had just swept through Cairo, and the estates of emirs who died of plague were seized for the treasury. A chronicler says the work cost 30,000 silver coins a day. Craftsmen came from all over the empire, and some of the stone is believed to come from the pyramids of Giza, which you saw on the 12th. Disaster struck in 1361, when one of the planned minarets collapsed and killed about 300 people, many of them children at a school below. Inside, four huge vaulted halls face the courtyard, said to be one for each of the four schools of Sunni law, with student lodgings packed into the corners. The building was so massive and so close to the Citadel that rebels used it as a fortress, and in 1517 the Ottomans bombarded it with cannon. As you go in, look high up on the great portal: parts of the carving were never finished.

summary: A royal mosque built to match Sultan Hassan across the lane, where Egypt's last kings and the last Shah of Iran are buried.
look: Across the narrow lane from Sultan Hassan, a building of similar height and colour with a dome and two minarets: from a distance most people cannot tell which one is medieval. Inside, the royal tombs lie in chambers around the prayer hall, richer and shinier than any Mamluk interior. Ask the guardian to point out the tombs of King Farouk and the Shah.
story:
The site once held a small Fatimid-era mosque, later a lodge of the Rifa'i Sufi order with the tomb of Ali Abu Shubbak, grandson of the order's founder, Ahmad al-Rifa'i. In 1869 Hoshiyar Qadin, mother of Khedive Ismail, commissioned a far bigger mosque to replace it and to serve as her family's mausoleum. Her architect, Hussein Fahmi Pasha, died during the first phase, work stopped after Ismail lost his throne, and Hoshiyar died in 1885. Khedive Abbas II restarted the project in 1905 under the Hungarian architect Max Herz, and it was finished in 1912.

It was designed in the neo-Mamluk style to stand level with Sultan Hassan, a way for the new dynasty to borrow medieval glory. Buried here are Hoshiyar, Khedive Ismail, Sultan Hussein Kamel, King Fuad I and King Farouk, the last king of Egypt, who died in exile in Rome in 1965. So is Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the last Shah of Iran, who died in Cairo in July 1980. His father, Reza Shah, also lay here from 1944 until 1950, when he was taken home to Iran.
details: Stand in the lane between the two mosques: the profiles match on purpose, built about 550 years apart.
King Farouk's tomb: the last reigning king of Egypt, who died in Rome in 1965.
The tomb of the last Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who died in Cairo in July 1980.
The shrine of the Sufi saint Ali Abu Shubbak al-Rifa'i, still visited by followers of the order.
fun_fact: The Shah's first wife was Princess Fawzia, King Farouk's sister; she and her father, King Fuad, are also listed among those buried here.
narration: The mosque facing Sultan Hassan looks medieval, but it was finished in 1912. It was commissioned in 1869 by Hoshiyar, the mother of Khedive Ismail, on the site of a small Sufi shrine, to be a mosque and a mausoleum for her family. Work stopped when Ismail lost his throne, and it was completed decades later under the Hungarian architect Max Herz. The builders deliberately matched the scale and style of Sultan Hassan across the lane, so that the new dynasty would stand shoulder to shoulder with Mamluk glory. Inside lie Hoshiyar herself, Khedive Ismail, King Fuad, and King Farouk, the last king of Egypt, who died in exile in Rome in 1965. And here too lies an unexpected guest: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the last Shah of Iran. After the revolution of 1979 he moved from country to country until Egypt took him in, and he died in Cairo in 1980. His first wife was Farouk's sister. Stand in the lane between the two mosques and compare them: the same height, the same mood, but about 550 years apart.

summary: For almost 700 years Egypt was ruled from this hilltop fortress, from Saladin to Khedive Ismail, and in 1811 it saw the massacre that ended the Mamluks.
look: The Citadel sits on a spur of the Muqattam hills above the old city. The Southern Enclosure holds the Muhammad Ali mosque, al-Nasir Muhammad's mosque, the Gawhara Palace and Joseph's Well; the Northern Enclosure, once the soldiers' quarter, holds the Military Museum. The terrace beside the Muhammad Ali mosque gives the great view west over Cairo. In 90 minutes: the Alabaster Mosque, al-Nasir Muhammad's mosque, the terrace, then the Gawhara Palace or the Military Museum.
story:
Saladin began the Citadel in 1176, a few years after abolishing the Fatimid caliphate, to defend Cairo against the Crusaders and give his new regime a safe seat. His eunuch and confidant Baha al-Din Qaraqush ran the works. Christian prisoners of war provided labour, and besides stone from the Muqattam hills Qaraqush quarried several of the small pyramids at Giza. An inscription on Bab al-Mudarraj, the only surviving original gate, dates completion to 1183-84.

Saladin's successors moved in, and the Mamluks filled the hill with palaces. Al-Nasir Muhammad built the striped Ablaq Palace, the domed Great Iwan and his mosque of 1318. After 1517 Selim I stripped the marble and shipped it to Istanbul, and the Citadel was divided between Ottoman garrison corps.

On 1 March 1811 Muhammad Ali invited the Mamluk leaders to a ceremony up here. As they rode down the narrow lane towards Bab al-Azab, his Albanian soldiers fired on them from above, and several hundred died. Legend says one bey leapt his horse over the wall and escaped. Muhammad Ali then demolished the Mamluk palaces and built his own mosque and palaces. In 1874 Khedive Ismail moved the government to Abdeen Palace, ending the Citadel's role as the seat of power. The British garrisoned it until 1946, and from 1983 it opened to visitors as a group of museums.
details: The terrace by the Muhammad Ali mosque: Sultan Hassan and al-Rifa'i right below, the old city beyond, Giza on the horizon.
Bab al-Azab (1754), the lower western gate: the sunken lane leading to it is where the Mamluks were shot in 1811.
Al-Nasir Muhammad's mosque (1318): the only major Mamluk building left on the hill.
Northern Enclosure: the Military Museum in Muhammad Ali's Harem Palace, with a MiG-21 jet outside.
Also inside: the Carriage Museum and the Police Museum in the old prison. Skip them if time is short.
fun_fact: Saladin's builders took stone from small pyramids at Giza, so some of the walls around you are recycled from the plateau you saw on the 12th.
narration: You are on the Citadel, the fortress from which Egypt was ruled for almost 700 years. Saladin began it in 1176, a few years after ending the Fatimid caliphate, to protect Cairo from the Crusaders and to keep his own new regime safe. His right-hand man, the eunuch Qaraqush, ran the works. Christian prisoners of war did much of the labour, and Qaraqush took stone from several of the small pyramids at Giza, so some of these walls are made of what you saw on the 12th. Mamluk sultans later filled the hilltop with palaces, and the Ottomans shipped their marble off to Istanbul. Then, on the first of March 1811, came the Citadel's darkest day. Muhammad Ali, the new ruler, invited the Mamluk leaders to a ceremony up here. As they rode down the narrow lane to the lower gate, his soldiers opened fire from above, and several hundred were killed. Legend says one bey leapt his horse over the wall and escaped. With his rivals gone, Muhammad Ali rebuilt the Citadel in his own image, and his family ruled from here until 1874. Now walk to the terrace beside the great mosque and look west: the old city lies below you, and on a clear day the pyramids stand on the horizon.

summary: Cairo's skyline signature is an Istanbul-style mosque, built by an Ottoman officer from Kavala to show Egypt it had a new, non-Mamluk master.
look: Visitors usually come in through a side gate into a big arcaded courtyard faced with alabaster, with a domed ablution fountain in the middle and an iron clock tower over the wall opposite the prayer hall. The prayer hall is almost square, about 45 by 46 metres, under a central dome 52 metres high, with four half-domes, four corner domes and rings of hanging lamps. Muhammad Ali's tomb is in its western corner, near the courtyard wall, behind a bronze screen.
story:
Muhammad Ali was born in 1769 in Kavala, in today's northern Greece. He came to Egypt with the Albanian troops of the Ottoman army sent against the French, made himself ruler in 1805, destroyed the Mamluks in 1811 and set about building a modern army and state. On the highest point of Cairo, after clearing the ruined Mamluk palaces, he began a mosque in 1830 that would look nothing like the Mamluk city below. A neo-Mamluk design by the French architect Pascal Coste was rejected; the building took the form of Istanbul's imperial mosques, such as the Sultan Ahmed and Şehzade mosques. The architect is uncertain: some sources name Yusuf Bushnaq from Istanbul, others suggest a Greek or an Armenian.

Muhammad Ali insisted on alabaster, partly to revive a declining local industry, so the lower walls and courtyard are faced with it. The upper panels were removed before completion and reused in the palaces of his successor Abbas I. The minarets rise over 80 metres.

The clock tower was a gift from King Louis-Philippe of France around 1846, in exchange for the Luxor obelisk that has stood in the Place de la Concorde in Paris since 1836. The clock was long out of order until King Farouk had it repaired.

Muhammad Ali died in 1849; his body was moved here in 1857, when the decoration was finished under his son Said. By the 1930s the domes were cracking, and between 1935 and 1939 they were dismantled and rebuilt to the original design.
details: Muhammad Ali's tomb: Carrara marble behind a bronze openwork screen, in the prayer hall's western corner by the courtyard wall.
The clock tower over the courtyard: Louis-Philippe's gift of about 1846, paid for with a Luxor obelisk.
Two pencil minarets of over 80 metres, Ottoman style, each with two balconies and a conical cap.
Two pulpits: the tall original wooden minbar, and King Farouk's smaller alabaster one of 1939.
The ablution fountain in the courtyard: carved marble under a wooden canopy, in a Baroque taste.
fun_fact: France got a Ramesses II obelisk more than 3,000 years old; Egypt got a clock that did not keep working for long. You will see the obelisk's twin at Luxor Temple on the 22nd.
narration: This is the mosque of Muhammad Ali, the domes and pencil minarets you see from all over Cairo. Muhammad Ali was an Ottoman officer born in 1769 in Kavala, in today's northern Greece. He came to Egypt with Albanian troops to fight the French, made himself ruler in 1805, and in 1811 wiped out the Mamluks just below this hilltop. Then he cleared their ruined palaces away and, from 1830, built a mosque that looks like nothing the Mamluks built: a pure Istanbul design, modelled on the imperial mosques of the Ottoman capital. The message was clear. Egypt had a new dynasty, and it looked to Istanbul and to Europe. He insisted on facing it with Egyptian alabaster, to revive a local craft, which is why people call it the Alabaster Mosque. Out in the courtyard, the iron clock tower was a gift from King Louis-Philippe of France, given in return for an obelisk from Luxor Temple that now stands in Paris. Cairenes like to say the clock never worked properly. Muhammad Ali died in 1849 and lies inside. Go into the prayer hall and look for the bronze screen in the corner by the courtyard wall: behind it stands his marble tomb.

summary: The royal mosque of the Mamluk sultans, the only major Mamluk building left on the Citadel, with a minaret top tiled like a Persian mosque.
look: A short walk from the Muhammad Ali mosque stands a plain, crenellated block about 63 by 57 metres around an open courtyard. Inside, the arcades rest on reused columns of every size and style, and the dome over the prayer niche stands on red granite columns. The minaret above the main entrance ends in a bulbous, garlic-shaped top sheathed in green, white and blue faience.
story:
Al-Nasir Muhammad, son of Qalawun, finished the mosque in 1318 as the Citadel's royal mosque, where the sultans came for Friday prayers. He prayed here daily, using a side room behind an iron grille as his private retreat, and he chose preachers by making each candidate preach in front of him. The endowment was so generous that the surplus bought land and shops. Ibn Battuta praised his virtue; the chronicles add that he was short and lame, with a cataract in one eye.

In 1335 the walls were raised, the roof rebuilt, and a green-tiled dome set over the prayer niche. The walls are said to use limestone taken from the pyramids, and the ten red granite columns came from ancient temples. The faience-covered minaret top is unique in Cairo; it was probably made by a craftsman from Tabriz, in Mongol-ruled Iran, at a time when al-Nasir was on friendly terms with the Mongols.

After 1517 Selim I carried off its marble panelling to Istanbul, the dome collapsed, and the arcades were walled up as prison cells and storerooms. In the British period an army officer, Charles Moore Watson, had prisoners strip out the plaster walls. Today it is open but seldom crowded.
details: The minaret over the main entrance: a garlic-shaped top in green, white and blue faience, unique in Cairo.
The arcades: columns of every size and style, pulled from older buildings. Compare the mismatched capitals.
Under the dome by the mihrab: red granite columns taken from ancient Egyptian temples.
Over the doors: inscriptions naming al-Nasir Muhammad son of Qalawun and the Hijra year 718, that is 1318.
The bare upper walls: the marble dado was stripped and shipped to Istanbul by Selim I after 1517.
fun_fact: This was the sultans' Friday mosque, and al-Nasir Muhammad auditioned his preachers personally: every candidate had to give a sermon in front of him.
narration: While everyone queues for the Alabaster Mosque, this plainer building is the real survivor: the mosque of al-Nasir Muhammad, the only major Mamluk monument left on the Citadel. Al-Nasir Muhammad, son of Qalawun, finished it in 1318 as the royal mosque of the palace, where the sultans came for Friday prayers, and he enlarged it in 1335. He chose his preachers in person, making each candidate deliver a sermon in front of him. Chroniclers describe him as short and lame, with a cataract in one eye, yet his reign was the high point of Mamluk Cairo. Inside, the arcades stand on columns of every size, collected from older buildings, and the dome rests on red granite columns from ancient temples. After the Ottoman conquest of 1517, Sultan Selim stripped its marble panelling and shipped it to Istanbul, and later the mosque served as a prison and storehouse. Now look up at the minaret over the main entrance: its bulging top is covered in green, white and blue tiles, a Persian touch probably brought by a craftsman from Tabriz.

summary: Muhammad Ali's reception palace, built by craftsmen from Greece, Turkey, Bulgaria and Albania, where he received envoys on a throne from Italy.
look: A two-storey Ottoman-style pavilion just south of the Muhammad Ali mosque, with European windows and terraces looking west over the city. Inside, the reception hall holds his throne, a huge chandelier and paintings of foreign ambassadors being received.
story:
Muhammad Ali commissioned the palace in 1814, three years after the massacre of the Mamluks a short way down the hill. Craftsmen from Greece, Turkey, Bulgaria and Albania built it as a Turkish-style kiosk, and the French architect Pascal Coste later added quarters for servants and officials. The name, Gawhara, means 'jewel', and it is often said to honour one of his wives.

Fire destroyed the wooden building in 1822, and gunpowder explosions caused another in 1824. Each time he rebuilt it grander, with Italian marble, terraces, orange groves and a menagerie with a lion, two tigers and an elephant. In the divan, the reception hall, he received guests under a 1,000 kg chandelier sent by King Louis-Philippe of France. The palace was damaged again by fire in 1972.
details: The throne: a gift to Muhammad Ali from the King of Italy.
The 1,000 kg chandelier in the reception hall, sent by Louis-Philippe of France.
Paintings of foreign ambassadors being presented to the pasha.
From the terraces: the old city and, on clear days, the pyramids.
fun_fact: In 1825 an English visitor, Anne Elwood, described a grand room here for dancing, with deep niches for conversation and side rooms for music, reading, games and refreshments.
narration: This elegant pavilion is the Gawhara Palace, built in 1814 for Muhammad Ali, three years after he massacred the Mamluks a short way down this hill. Craftsmen from Greece, Turkey, Bulgaria and Albania built it in Turkish style, with European windows and a view over the whole city. Here the pasha received foreign ambassadors, sitting on a throne given by the King of Italy, under a huge chandelier sent by the King of France. Fire damaged the palace more than once, and each time he rebuilt it grander. Inside, look for the throne and the paintings of envoys being presented to him.

summary: A well about 85 metres deep, cut through the rock for Saladin's Citadel, where oxen walked down a spiral ramp to turn the waterwheels.
look: In the Southern Enclosure, a square opening in the rock with a wide upper shaft wrapped by a spiral passage. It is usually closed to visitors, but you may be able to look down from the top.
story:
A fortress on a dry hill needs water that no besieger can cut off. Saladin's overseer Baha al-Din Qaraqush, who also built the walls, had a well dug through the rock, about 85 metres deep. It is called Bir Yusuf, after Saladin's own first name, Yusuf, the Arabic form of Joseph, not after the Joseph of the Bible, though guides happily tell both stories.

The well works in two stages. A spiral stair winds round the wide upper shaft, and it could be covered with earth to make a ramp for oxen. At the bottom of the upper section two oxen turned a waterwheel; a second wheel at the top, also driven by oxen, lifted the water the rest of the way.
details: The spiral passage round the upper shaft: oxen once walked down it to their waterwheel.
The name: Yusuf was Saladin's birth name, the Arabic form of Joseph.
Usually locked: ask at the gate, but do not count on going down.
fun_fact: Its other name, Bir al-Halazon, means the Snail Well, after the spiral passage coiled round the shaft.
narration: This opening in the rock is Joseph's Well, one of the cleverest works on the Citadel. A fortress on a dry hill needs water that no besieger can cut off, so Saladin's builder Qaraqush had a shaft cut down through the rock, about 85 metres deep. It is called Bir Yusuf after Saladin himself, whose first name was Yusuf, the Arabic Joseph, not after the Joseph of the Bible. A spiral ramp winds around the upper shaft, and oxen walked down it to turn a waterwheel deep inside, while a second team at the top lifted the water the rest of the way. It is usually closed, but if you can, look down into the spiral.
